mainTopic: False oaths and denials about money: worthless חמץ, the guardian claim, witnesses' oaths, and רב ששת's rule about a שומר who denies a deposit.
overview: רבא asks about a robber who swore falsely about stolen חמץ that became forbidden after פסח and is now worthless. Does that oath count as denying money? The גמרא answers from רבה: someone accused of stealing an ox who falsely claims to be a שומר or a borrower is liable, because he freed himself from a possible future payment. So the חמץ oath also counts as denying money. רב עמרם objects from a ברייתא that exempts a מודה בעיקר, and רבא answers that the ברייתא is about an ox handed back on the spot, while his case is about an ox still out in a swamp. The גמרא then explains how several claims in that ברייתא count as admitting the main claim. Next comes בן עזאי's list of false witness oaths about a lost item, and a dispute over whether a single witness is liable, which depends on whether a דבר הגורם לממון counts as money. Finally, רב ששת rules that a שומר who denies a deposit becomes a גזלן. A proof for him is pushed aside, and רמי בר חמא's challenge is answered by explaining that a denial made only to stall is not real כפירה. The support for that answer, from one who denies a loan, continues on the next amud.

steps.title: What if the robber swore falsely about the forbidden חמץ?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether a false oath about stolen חמץ, now worthless after פסח, counts as denying money.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he swore about it, what is the law? Do we say: since he would have to pay if it got stolen, he is denying money? Or perhaps: right now it is just sitting here and is mere dust, so he is not denying money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues רבא's case of the robbed חמץ. It asks whether a false oath about it brings the penalties of a false oath about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Side one: the robber is still responsible if the חמץ gets stolen, so a real money obligation is at stake. Side two: the item itself is worthless right now, and he could simply hand it back as-is, so nothing of value is being denied.

phrases.english: If he swore about it, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the stolen חמץ, which became forbidden once פסח passed.

phrases.english: Do we say:
since if it were stolen
he would need to pay him,
so he is denying him money;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא, הַשְׁתָּא מִיהַת הָא מַנַּח
phrases.english: or perhaps, now at any rate, it is lying right here
and it is just dust,
and he has not denied him money?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a follow-up question to רבא's earlier ruling about robbed חמץ.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a possible future obligation to pay, if the item is stolen, make a false oath about a worthless item into a denial of money?

steps.title: רבה already treats this as obvious: the ox case begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבה considers רבא's question obvious and starts quoting his case about an accused ox thief.
steps.simpleTranslation: What was a question for רבא is obvious to רבה. For רבה said: one says, 'You stole my ox,' and the other says, 'I did not steal it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings רבה's ruling to answer רבא's question. This line only sets up the case; the ruling comes in the next steps.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The setup is a man accused of stealing an ox who denies the theft. The point will be what he claims instead, and what that claim lets him avoid paying.

keyTerms.meaning: it was a question for him

steps.confusionAlert: רָבָא and רַבָּה are two different אמוראים with almost the same name. רבה lived earlier, and here he already settles what רבא was asking.

phrases.english: The matter that was a question for Rava
is obvious to Rabba,
as Rabba says:
One says, 'You stole my ox,'
and he says, 'I did not steal it.'

steps.triggerLanguage: מִילְּתָא דְּאִיבַּעְיָא לֵיהּ לְרָבָא, פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ לְרַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces רבה's ruling as the answer to רבא's question.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup: an accused ox thief denies stealing it.

steps.title: Claiming to be an unpaid guard makes him liable
steps.stepSummary: If the accused claims to be an unpaid guard and swears falsely, he is liable, since he freed himself from paying for theft and loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'What is it doing with you?' 'I am an unpaid guard over it.' He is liable, because he exempted himself from theft and loss.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה rules that the accused, who says he is only an unpaid guard, is liable for his false oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thief must pay if the ox is later stolen or lost, but an unpaid guard does not. The ox is right there, yet by lying he escaped a possible future payment, and רבה counts that as denying money. The same reasoning fits רבא's חמץ: a possible duty to pay if it is stolen counts as money.

keyTerms.meaning: unpaid guard, who is not responsible for theft or loss

phrases.english: 'Then what is it doing with you?'
'I am an unpaid guard over it.'
He is liable,
phrases.notes: Liable for a false oath about money: he brings a קרבן אשם if he swore and later admitted the truth.

phrases.english: because he exempted himself
from theft and loss.

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם אֲנִי עָלָיו – חַיָּיב, שֶׁהֲרֵי פָּטַר עַצְמוֹ מִגְּנֵיבָה וַאֲבֵידָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבה's ruling for the case set up in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's question about the false oath over forbidden חמץ
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבה: denying a possible future duty to pay counts as denying money, even when the item itself is present.

steps.title: Claiming to be a paid guard also makes him liable
steps.stepSummary: If he claims to be a paid guard and swears falsely, he is liable too, since he freed himself from paying for breakage and death.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I am a paid guard over it.' He is liable, because he exempted himself from breakage and death.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה gives the second version of the claim, a paid guard, and rules that he is also liable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A paid guard does pay for theft and loss, but not for accidents like the animal breaking a limb or dying. A thief pays even for those. So this claim also escapes a possible future payment, which again counts as denying money.

keyTerms.meaning: paid guard, who is not responsible for accidents
an animal that broke a limb or died

steps.whatToRemember: For רבה, denying even a possible future duty to pay is denying money. So in רבא's case, a false oath about the worthless חמץ counts as a false oath about money, because the robber would have to pay if it were stolen.

phrases.english: If he says, 'I am a paid guard over it,'
he is liable,
because he exempted himself
from breakage and death.

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹמֵר שָׂכָר אֲנִי עָלָיו – חַיָּיב, שֶׁהֲרֵי פָּטַר עַצְמוֹ מִשְּׁבוּרָה וּמֵתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel second case in רבה's ruling, using the same reasoning.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's question about the false oath over forbidden חמץ
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבה: the paid-guard claim escapes liability for accidents, which counts as denying money.

steps.title: The borrower claim also makes him liable
steps.stepSummary: If the accused falsely swears he borrowed the ox, he is liable, since he freed himself from paying if it dies from normal work.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he says, 'I am a borrower of it,' and swore falsely, he is liable, because he exempted himself from paying in case the ox dies from its regular work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the third and last version of רבה's case. Here the accused claims to be a borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower pays for almost everything, so this claim releases him from very little: only death caused by normal work. Even that small release counts as denying money, so he is still liable. This completes the pattern from steps 3 and 4.

keyTerms.meaning: A borrower, who must pay for nearly any loss
An animal that died because of its normal work
He exempted himself (from having to pay)

phrases.english: "I am a borrower of it" – he is liable,
since he exempted himself
from [paying if it] died because of work.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third case in רבה's list, after the unpaid guard and the paid guard
steps.raayaObject: That a false guardian claim on an ox still present counts as denying money
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבה's statement about the accused ox thief

steps.title: Applying רבה's principle to the worthless חמץ
steps.stepSummary: Even though the ox is still there, the oath denies money because of a possible future theft. So too, the worthless חמץ was worth full money if stolen, so the oath denies money.
steps.simpleTranslation: It seems that even though the ox is still standing there, since he would be denying money if it were stolen, he is denying money now too. Here too, even though the חמץ is just dust, since he would have to pay real money if it had been stolen, he is denying him money now too.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pulls the general principle out of רבה's cases and uses it to answer רבא's question about the חמץ.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבה's cases nothing is lost right now. The oath counts as denying money because of what it would save him in a possible situation. Likewise, the חמץ is worthless now, but the oath still concerns a real money obligation, so it counts as denying money and he is liable.
steps.whatToRemember: An oath can count as denying money even when nothing is lost right now. It is enough that the oath would free him from a real money obligation.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the oath is about the ox's current value. The point is what the oath would let him escape paying if something happened.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the answer to רבא's question in step 1. It is also the rule that רב עמרם is about to challenge.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא אַף עַל גַּב דְּהָא קָאֵים –
phrases.english: Apparently, even though this [ox] is standing [here] –
since if it would be stolen
he would be denying money,
now too he is denying money;
here too, even though
phrases.notes: "Here" goes back to רבא's question about the stolen חמץ.

phrases.english: it is mere dust –
since if it had been stolen
he would have to pay him real money,

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא נָמֵי מָמוֹנָא קָא כָפַר לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: now too he is denying him money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא אַף עַל גַּב דְּהָא קָאֵים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the principle from רבה's three cases and applies it to רבא's question
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A false oath about חמץ that became worthless still counts as denying money, so he is liable.

steps.title: רב עמרם objects from 'וכחש בה'
steps.stepSummary: When רבא taught this rule, רב עמרם challenged him with a ברייתא saying that someone who admits the main part of the claim is excluded.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא sat and taught this rule. רב עמרם objected to רבא: "And he denies it" excludes someone who admits the main thing.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא teaches the rule, and רב עמרם starts an objection by quoting a ברייתא. This step sets up the challenge, and the ברייתא's details come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא learns from the פסוק that the oath must deny the main claim. In רבה's cases, the man admits he has the owner's ox and only lies about how he got it. That looks like admitting the main thing, which the ברייתא says does not make him liable.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him (from a source)
And he denies it (the פסוק about a false money oath)
One who admits the main part of the claim

phrases.english: Rava sat and was saying
this teaching.
phrases.notes: The rule just explained: a false guardian oath counts as denying money.

phrases.english: Rav Amram raised an objection to Rava:
"And he denies it" –
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:22

phrases.english: excluding one who admits to the main thing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the principle just concluded
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a false guardian oath, on an ox still present, counts as denying money
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא excludes someone who admits the main claim. The guardian-claimer admits the ox belongs to the owner, so he should not be liable.

steps.title: The ברייתא begins its example
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא starts explaining its case: the owner says 'You stole my ox,' and the other says 'I did not steal it.'
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? He says, "You stole my ox," and the other says, "I did not steal it."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא starts describing exactly what kind of case it means. The rest of its explanation comes in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case is set up just like רבה's: an owner accuses someone of stealing his ox. This parallel is what gives the objection its force. We need the rest of the ברייתא to see how it treats the denial.

phrases.english: How so? "You stole my ox,"
and he says: "I did not steal [it]";

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues quoting the ברייתא that רב עמרם uses for his objection
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's ruling, as taught by רבא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's example uses the same ox-theft setup as רבה's cases, preparing to show that admitting the main thing removes liability.

steps.title: The list of answers the accused might give
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. The owner asks why the ox is with the other person, and the ברייתא lists ten possible answers, including being a שומר or a borrower.
steps.simpleTranslation: The owner asks: 'What is my ox doing with you?' The other answers with one of these: 'You sold it to me.' 'You gave it to me as a gift.' 'Your father sold it to me.' 'Your father gave it to me as a gift.' 'It ran after my cow.' 'It came to me by itself.' 'I found it lost on the road.' 'I am an unpaid שומר over it.' 'I am a paid שומר over it.' 'I am borrowing it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still quoting רב עמרם's ברייתא. Here it lists the different stories the accused might tell to explain why he has the ox. The ruling about these answers comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Look at the last three answers: unpaid שומר, paid שומר and borrower are exactly the cases רבה ruled create liability, and רבא taught that ruling (Steps 3-5). That is why this ברייתא is a strong challenge. In every answer, the accused agrees that the ox is with him and is not denying the theft completely.

keyTerms.meaning: What is it doing with you? (What is your connection to it?)

phrases.english: "What is it doing with you?"
"You sold it to me";
"You gave it to me as a gift";
"Your father sold it to me";
"Your father gave it to me as a gift";
"It ran after my cow";
"It came to me by itself";
"I found it lost on the road";
"I am an unpaid guard over it";
"I am a paid guard over it";
"I am a borrower of it" —

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's case from Step 8 by listing the accused's possible explanations.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule, taught by רבא (Steps 3-6), that a false oath of being an unpaid שומר, a paid שומר or a borrower makes one liable.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא lists those very same claims, which sets up its ruling that they are exempt.

steps.title: The verse exempts someone who admits the main claim
steps.stepSummary: After he swears to one of these answers and later admits it was false, he is exempt, because 'וכחש בה' excludes someone who is מודה בעיקר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He swore to one of these, and then admitted it was a lie. You might think he should be liable. So the פסוק says 'and he denies it', which excludes someone who admits the main claim.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the punch line of רב עמרם's challenge. The ברייתא says that a person who swore falsely to any of these stories is NOT liable for a false oath about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the accused admits the ox is really the owner's, he has not denied the main claim. So the ברייתא rules he is exempt even when he claimed to be a paid שומר or a borrower. That clashes directly with רבא, who said these claims do deny money.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who admits the main point of the claim

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the accused is exempt because he told the truth. He did lie under oath. He is exempt from the special payment for a false oath because he admitted the main fact: the ox really belongs to the owner.

phrases.english: and he swore and then admitted;
one might think he should be liable?
The verse says: "and he denies it" —
phrases.notes: ויקרא 5:22

phrases.english: this excludes one who admits the main claim.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling about the list of answers in Step 9, completing the challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule, taught by רבא, from Steps 3-6.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא explicitly exempts someone who falsely swore he was a paid שומר or a borrower, but רבא said he is liable.

steps.title: רבא: the ox was handed back, not left in a swamp
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the ברייתא is a case where the accused says 'Here it is' and returns the ox right away. רבא's own case is where the ox is out in a swamp.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Fool! That ברייתא is talking about when he says 'Here it is, take it.' When I spoke, I meant a case where the ox is standing out in a swamp.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רב עמרם's challenge by showing that the ברייתא and his rule are talking about two different situations.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ox is handed back on the spot, saying 'I was a שומר' gains nothing, because the owner already has his ox and there is no future risk. If the ox is still out in a swamp, it could still be stolen or die. Claiming to be a שומר then frees the person from paying for that, so the oath really does deny money.
steps.whatToRemember: A false claim of being a שומר denies money only when the item is not right there to return. If he says 'הילך' and hands it over, there is nothing left to deny.

phrases.english: He said to him: Fool!
phrases.notes: רבא is answering רב עמרם.

phrases.english: When that ברייתא was taught —
it was where he said to him: "Here it is,"
when I said my rule —
it was where it is standing in a swamp.
phrases.notes: The ox is not in front of them, so it is still at risk of being lost or stolen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: תְּדוֹרָא! כִּי תַּנְיָא הָהִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from Steps 7-10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the ברייתא and רבא are talking about different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to exempt every false claim of being a שומר or a borrower.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא exempts only when the ox is handed back at once. When the ox is away in a swamp, רבא's rule of liability stands.

steps.title: How is 'You sold it to me' an admission?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how 'You sold it to me' counts as admitting the main claim, since he is claiming the ox is his.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You sold it to me': what admission of the main claim is there in that?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא's list and questions one item in it. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'you sold it to me' sounds like a full denial: the ox is mine, not yours. So it is hard to see why the ברייתא calls him מודה בעיקר.

phrases.english: "You sold it to me" —
what admission of the main claim is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to analyze items in the ברייתא quoted in Steps 9-10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a claim of buying the ox can count as admitting it belongs to the owner.

steps.title: He bought it but never paid
steps.stepSummary: The case is where he says: 'You sold it to me, but I never paid you, so take your ox and go.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed for a case where he said to him: 'I did not give you the money. Take your ox and go.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 12 by describing a specific case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he admits he never paid, the sale never went through, and he gives the ox back. That is an admission that the ox belongs to the owner, so he is מודה בעיקר.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for (this case)

phrases.english: It is needed only,
where he said to him: "I did not give you the money,
take your ox and go."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He admits he never paid and returns the ox, so he admits it is the owner's.

steps.title: How is 'You gave it to me' an admission?
steps.stepSummary: The same question about the gift claims: 'You gave it to me' and 'Your father gave it to me'. How do these admit the main claim?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'You gave it to me'; 'Your father gave it to me': what admission of the main claim is there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question about the gift answers in the list. The answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A gift has no price, so the answer from Step 13 ('I didn't pay') does not work here. A new explanation is needed.

phrases.english: "You gave it to me"; "Your father gave it to me" —
what admission of the main claim is there?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same question from Step 12 to the gift claims.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How a claim of receiving the ox as a gift can count as admitting it belongs to the owner.

steps.title: A gift on a condition that was not kept
steps.stepSummary: The case is where he says: 'It was given on condition that I do something to please you. I didn't do it, so take your ox and go.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Where he said to him: 'It was given to me on condition that I do something to please you, and I didn't do it for you. Take your ox and go.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 14 by describing a gift that had a condition attached.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the condition was never kept, the gift never took effect. By returning the ox he admits it belongs to the owner, so he is מודה בעיקר.

keyTerms.meaning: Satisfaction, something that pleases a person

steps.whatToRemember: Each claim in the ברייתא counts as מודה בעיקר because, in the end, the accused admits the ox belongs to the owner and gives it back ('שקול תורך וזיל').

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: ״עַל מְנָת דְּעָבֵידְנָא לָךְ נְיָיח דְּנַפְשָׁא,
phrases.english: where he said to him: "On condition that I do something to please you,
and I did not do it for you,
take your ox and go."

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: עַל מְנָת דְּעָבֵידְנָא לָךְ נְיָיח דְּנַפְשָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The gift had a condition that was never kept, so he admits the ox is the owner's and returns it.

steps.title: The owner can answer: you should have returned it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא looks at the last excuse, 'I found it straying on the road.' The owner can simply reply that the finder was obligated to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he says, 'I found it straying on the road,' let the owner say to him: 'You should have returned it to me!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the case of 'I found it straying,' just as it questioned the earlier excuses in steps 12 and 14. Saying 'I found it' does not seem to help him, because a finder must return a lost item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the other excuses, the גמרא had to explain how the person was admitting the owner's main claim. Here the problem is that 'I found it' is not much of a defense. Anyone who finds a lost animal has a duty to give it back, so the owner can say, 'Then why didn't you return it?'

keyTerms.meaning: Straying on the road (a lost animal)

phrases.english: "I found it straying on the road"
Let him say: You should have returned it to me!
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the owner of the ox, answering the person who has it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of questions about each excuse, now reaching the last one, 'I found it.'
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the excuse 'I found it straying' works, since the owner can reply that a finder must return the item.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's inclusion of 'I found it straying on the road' as an exempt case of מודה בעיקר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A finder must return a lost item, so the owner can retort 'You should have returned it to me.' Claiming to be a finder therefore does not seem to give the accused a real defense.

steps.title: He swore he did not know the ox was the owner's
steps.stepSummary: אבוה דשמואל explains that the person swore he found a lost item and did not know it belonged to this owner, so he could not have returned it to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל's father said: This is where he says, 'I swear that I found a lost item, and I did not know it was yours so that I could return it to you.'
steps.whatsHappening: אבוה דשמואל answers the question by making the case more specific. The person swore that he did not know whose ox it was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner's reply, 'You should have returned it,' only works if the finder knew who the owner was. In this case the finder swears he did not know, so he did nothing wrong by keeping it. That makes the excuse a real defense.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath (here, the opening words of his oath: 'I swear')

steps.whatToRemember: Each excuse in the list (I bought it, it was a gift, I found it) was explained as a specific case so that it fits the ברייתא. For 'I found it,' the person swore he did not know who the owner was.

phrases.english: Shmuel's father said:
It is where he says: "I swear that I found a lost item,"
and I did not know that it was yours
so that I could return it to you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 16 by spelling out exactly what the person swore.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The person swore he found a lost item and did not know it belonged to this owner, so he had no way to return it to him.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): the finder swore he did not know whose ox it was.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The finder claim seemed to give no defense, since a finder must return the item.
steps.terutzMaskana: He swore he did not know the ox belonged to this owner, so he had no way to return it, and the ברייתא's case stands.

steps.title: בן עזאי: three false oaths about a lost item
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes בן עזאי listing three cases where a witness's oath that he knows nothing about a lost item is false.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: בן עזאי said: There are three oaths. He recognized the item but not its finder; he recognized its finder but not the item; he recognized neither the item nor its finder.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא on a related topic. A witness swore he knew nothing about a lost item, and בן עזאי lists three ways that oath could be false.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witness swore he had no information at all. בן עזאי says the oath is false even if he knew only part of the story, such as the item but not who found it, or the finder but not the item. The third case in the list looks strange, and the גמרא deals with it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A תנא (sage of the משנה period)

phrases.english: It was taught: Ben Azzai said:
There are three oaths:
he recognized it but not its finder,
its finder but not it,
neither it nor its finder.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the oath of the person holding the ox to a new ברייתא about witnesses' oaths concerning a lost item.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A witness's oath that he knows nothing about a lost item is false in three cases where he actually knew something.

steps.title: If he recognized neither, he swore the truth
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the third case: if he knew neither the item nor the finder, his oath was true.
steps.simpleTranslation: Neither the item nor its finder?! Then he swore the truth!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the third case in בן עזאי's list. A witness who knew nothing and swore he knew nothing did not lie.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list is supposed to give cases of false oaths. Someone who recognized neither the item nor the finder told the truth, so this case does not belong on the list.

phrases.english: Neither it nor its finder?!
He swore the truth!

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא בָּהּ וְלֹא בְּמוֹצְאָהּ?! קוּשְׁטָא אִשְׁתְּבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the third case in the ברייתא of step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The third case of בן עזאי, where he recognized neither the item nor its finder.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A person who knew nothing and swore he knew nothing swore truthfully, so this cannot be a false oath.

steps.title: Correct it: he recognized both
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא changes the wording of the third case to say that he recognized both the item and its finder.
steps.simpleTranslation: Say instead: he recognized both the item and its finder.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the problem by reading the third case differently. It becomes a case where the witness knew everything.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the corrected wording, all three cases are false oaths. The witness knew only the item, or only the finder, or both, yet he swore he knew nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: Say (read the text this way instead)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not count 'neither the item nor the finder' as one of the three false oaths. The גמרא corrects that case to 'both the item and the finder.'

phrases.english: Say: it and its finder.
phrases.notes: The גמרא is changing the wording, so read the third case as 'he recognized both.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 19 by changing the wording of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The third case was read as a witness who recognized nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The third case is a witness who recognized both the item and its finder.

steps.title: What law do these cases teach?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical law בן עזאי meant to teach with his three cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: For which law were these cases taught?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what follows in practice from בן עזאי's three cases. This question sets up the disagreement in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists the cases but does not say what result they have. The גמרא wants to know whether they teach that the witness is liable or that he is exempt.

phrases.english: For which halakha?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Now that the three cases are settled, the גמרא asks what law they teach.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical law that בן עזאי's three cases teach.

steps.title: Exempt or liable: רבי חנינא and שמואל disagree
steps.stepSummary: רב אמי, quoting רבי חנינא, says the cases teach that the witness is exempt. שמואל says they teach that he is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אמי said in the name of רבי חנינא: to teach that he is exempt. And שמואל said: to teach that he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question with opposite views. One says the cases teach פטור and the other says they teach חיוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The issue is whether the witness must bring a קרבן for a false oath of testimony. According to רבי חנינא he is exempt in these cases, and according to שמואל he is liable to bring the קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who quotes רבי חנינא
An early אמורא in ארץ ישראל

steps.whatToRemember: בן עזאי lists three false oaths of a witness: he knew the item, or the finder, or both. רבי חנינא says these cases are exempt from a קרבן, and שמואל says they require one.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: לִפְטוּר,
phrases.english: Rav Ami says in the name of Rabbi Ḥanina: to teach exemption,
phrases.notes: Exempt from bringing a קרבן for a false oath of testimony.

phrases.english: and Shmuel says: to teach liability.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא: לִפְטוּר, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר: לְחִיּוּב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 21 with two opposite opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי חנינא: the cases teach exemption from a קרבן. שמואל: they teach liability to bring a קרבן.

steps.title: The argument matches an older dispute between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says that רב אמי and שמואל are arguing about the same thing as an earlier dispute in a ברייתא about a single witness who is made to swear.
steps.simpleTranslation: Their argument is the same as the argument of these תנאים, as a ברייתא teaches: if someone makes a single witness swear, the witness is exempt. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון says he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the argument between רב אמי and שמואל from the last step is not new. תנאים already argued about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A single witness cannot force anyone to pay, because it takes two witnesses for that. So when he falsely swears he knows nothing, it is unclear whether his oath is about money. The תנא קמא exempts him, and רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון holds him liable. This lines up with רב אמי (exempt) and שמואל (liable).

keyTerms.meaning: One who makes someone take an oath

phrases.english: And [they argue] in the dispute of these tanna'im,
phrases.notes: "They" means רב אמי and שמואל from the previous step.

phrases.english: as it is taught in a baraita:
One who makes a single witness swear — [the witness] is exempt,
phrases.notes: Exempt from the קרבן that a witness brings for a false oath that he knows no testimony.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon holds him liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Anchors the אמוראים's dispute from step 22 in an earlier dispute between תנאים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא exempts a single witness who swore falsely. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון holds him liable.

steps.title: What is the root of their argument?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what idea the two תנאים are really arguing about.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are they arguing about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the underlying reason behind the dispute. It is setting up the explanation that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knowing who says exempt and who says liable is not enough. The גמרא wants the principle that drives each side.

phrases.english: About what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind the dispute quoted in step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that divides the תנא קמא and רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון.

steps.title: Does something that causes money count as money?
steps.stepSummary: One side holds that something that only causes money to be paid counts as money. The other side holds it does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds that something that causes money is considered like money. The other Sage holds it is not considered like money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the dispute. It turns on whether a דבר הגורם לממון counts as money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A single witness's testimony does not make anyone pay by itself. It can only lead to payment, for example by pushing the defendant to swear or to admit. רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון says that counts as a money matter, so the oath is about money and he is liable. The תנא קמא says it does not count, so he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Something that only causes money to be paid

steps.whatToRemember: The single-witness dispute depends on whether a דבר הגורם לממון counts as ממון. Liable (רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, like שמואל) says yes. Exempt (תנא קמא, like רב אמי) says no.

phrases.english: One Sage holds: something that causes money
phrases.notes: This first "Sage" is רבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון, who held the witness liable.

phrases.english: is considered like money,
and the other Sage holds: it is not considered like money.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר סָבַר: דָּבָר הַגּוֹרֵם לְמָמוֹן – כְּמָמוֹן דָּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree about whether a דבר הגורם לממון is considered ממון.

steps.title: A bailee who denies a deposit becomes a robber
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת rules that a שומר who falsely denies having a פקדון is treated as a גזלן and must pay even for accidents.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: one who denies a deposit becomes a robber regarding it, and he is liable even for accidents.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. רב ששת gives a rule about a שומר who lies and denies having the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a שומר is not responsible for אונסין, accidents beyond his control. Once he falsely denies having the item, he is treated like a thief who has taken it. A thief must pay no matter what happens to the stolen item.

keyTerms.meaning: One who denies holding a deposit

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
One who denies a deposit —
becomes a robber regarding it,
and is liable for accidents.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the liability of a שומר who denies the deposit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A כופר בפקדון becomes a גזלן and is liable even for אונסין.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to support רב ששת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא that speaks of a "punishment" for denying a deposit, and suggests this means a money penalty like רב ששת's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: A תנא also taught this: "And he denies it" teaches us the punishment. Where is the warning? The verse says: "You shall not deny." Is this not talking about a money punishment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to back up רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא finds a עונש (punishment) for denying a deposit and a separate אזהרה (warning). The גמרא suggests the punishment is a money penalty, meaning paying even for accidents, which is exactly רב ששת's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: And a תנא taught the same as us

phrases.english: And a tanna taught in line with us:
"And he denies it" — we learned the punishment.
phrases.notes: ויקרא ה:כב

phrases.english: From where is the warning?
The verse says: "You shall not deny."
phrases.notes: ויקרא יט:יא

phrases.english: What, is it not about a money punishment?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב ששת's rule from a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב ששת's rule that a כופר בפקדון pays for אונסין.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא learning a עונש from "וכחש בה", read as a money punishment.

steps.title: Maybe the punishment is for the oath
steps.stepSummary: The proof is pushed away: maybe the punishment in the ברייתא is for a false oath, not for the denial alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is about the punishment of the oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof by reading the ברייתא another way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the punishment is for swearing falsely, then the ברייתא does not show that denying alone turns the שומר into a גזלן. It would then give no support to רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: The punishment for a false oath

phrases.english: No, it is about the punishment of an oath.
phrases.notes: He means the penalties for swearing falsely about money, like the added fifth and a קרבן.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 27.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the reading that the ברייתא's punishment is a money penalty for denial alone.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The punishment could refer to a false oath rather than to the denial.

steps.title: The second part of the ברייתא is about the oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the second part of the ברייתא already covers the false oath. So the first part must be about denying without an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the last part teaches a case where he swore, it follows that the first part is where he did not swear. The last part says: "And he swears falsely" — we learned the punishment. Where is the warning? The verse says: "You shall not lie." Since the last part is where he swore, the first part is where he did not swear!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the rejection from step 28 and defends the proof for רב ששת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא has two parts. The second part is clearly about a false oath. If the first part were also about an oath, the two parts would repeat each other. So the first part must be about plain denial without an oath, and its punishment must be the money penalty, which supports רב ששת.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a teaching
The first part of a teaching

steps.confusionAlert: This step is not a new opinion. It argues against the rejection in step 28 and so brings back the proof for רב ששת.

phrases.english: But from the fact that the last part teaches where he swore,
it follows that the first part is where he did not swear —
as the last part teaches:
"And he swears falsely" — we learned the punishment.
phrases.notes: ויקרא ה:כב

phrases.english: From where is the warning?
The verse says: "You shall not lie."
phrases.notes: ויקרא יט:יא

phrases.english: And since the last part is where he swore,
the first part is where he did not swear!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מִדְּקָתָנֵי סֵיפָא וְאִישְׁתְּבַע, מִכְּלָל דְּרֵישָׁא דְּלָא אִישְׁתְּבַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rejection of step 28 and brings back the proof of step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rejection in step 28, which read the first part of the ברייתא as being about an oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The second part already covers the false oath. To avoid repeating itself, the first part must cover denial without an oath, so its punishment is monetary.

steps.title: Both parts of the ברייתא are about a false oath
steps.stepSummary: Both parts of the ברייתא deal with a שומר who swore. One part is where witnesses exposed him, so he pays for accidents. The other is where he admitted on his own, so he pays קרן, חומש and brings an אשם.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: both parts are talking about someone who swore. One part is where he admitted, and the other part is where witnesses came. If witnesses came, he must pay even for accidents. If he admitted on his own, he pays the principal, adds a fifth, and brings a guilt-offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the problem from step 29. The two parts of the ברייתא do not repeat each other, because they describe two different ways the false oath was uncovered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 29 claimed the first part must be about denial without an oath, since the second part already covers the oath. Now the גמרא shows both parts can be about an oath: the first is when witnesses caught him, the second is when he confessed. So the ברייתא gives no proof for רב ששת, and the דחיה of step 28 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that (both parts of the source)
Accidents beyond his control (theft by armed robbers, death of the animal, etc.)
The principal amount plus an extra fifth
A guilt-offering brought for a false oath about money

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two outcomes. When witnesses expose him, his punishment is having to pay even for accidents. When he admits on his own, he pays קרן, חומש and brings an אשם.

phrases.english: They say: both this and that are where he swore;
phrases.notes: "This and that" means both parts of the ברייתא from steps 27–29.

phrases.english: here, where he admitted;
there, where witnesses came.
If witnesses came, he is liable for accidents.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹדוֹיֵי אוֹדִי – חַיָּיב בְּקֶרֶן וְחוֹמֶשׁ וְאָשָׁם.
phrases.english: If he admitted, he is obligated in the principal, a fifth, and a guilt-offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 29 and restores the דחיה of step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: both parts are about an oath, but one is exposed by witnesses and the other by admission.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first part of the ברייתא must be about denial without an oath, since the second part covers the oath.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both parts are about an oath, so the ברייתא does not support רב ששת.
steps.whatToRemember: The attempted proof for רב ששת from the ברייתא fails. Both parts can be read as cases of a false oath.

steps.title: רמי בר חמא quotes the משנה about who is suspect on oaths
steps.stepSummary: רמי בר חמא quotes a משנה. It says a person becomes 'suspect on oaths' through a false oath of testimony, a false oath about a deposit, or even a vain oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: רמי בר חמא objects: 'And when his opponent is suspect on oaths.' How does he become suspect? Through an oath of testimony, an oath about a deposit, or even a vain oath.
steps.whatsHappening: A new challenge begins, this time against רב ששת's rule itself. Here the גמרא only quotes the source; the actual attack comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists cases where the plaintiff swears instead of the defendant, because the defendant is not trusted to swear. Every way of becoming 'suspect' on the list is a false oath. None of them is a simple denial.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection from a source
Suspected of swearing falsely, so not trusted to take an oath
A false oath that one has no testimony to give
A false oath denying that one holds a deposit
A pointless oath, such as swearing that something obvious is false

phrases.english: Rami bar Chama raises an objection:
"And where his opponent is suspect on oaths." How so?
phrases.notes: This is from the משנה in שבועות (44b). "His opponent" is the defendant, so the plaintiff swears and collects instead.

phrases.english: Whether an oath of testimony,
or an oath about a deposit,
and even a vain oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof for רב ששת failed, the גמרא now brings a source that seems to go against him.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only: the משנה lists only false oaths as the way to become 'suspect'. The attack itself comes in step 32.

steps.title: If denial makes him a גזלן, the denial should disqualify him
steps.stepSummary: If רב ששת is right that denial alone makes the שומר a גזלן, he should already be untrustworthy from the denial. The משנה, though, requires a false oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is so, then he should already be disqualified by the denial!
steps.whatsHappening: This is the actual attack on רב ששת, based on the משנה just quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזלן cannot be trusted to swear. If a false denial made the שומר a גזלן, the denial alone would make him 'suspect'. Yet the משנה lists only a false oath of a deposit, which suggests denial without an oath does not make him a גזלן.

keyTerms.meaning: And if it is so (if that rule were true)

phrases.english: And if it is so,
phrases.notes: He means: if רב ששת's rule were true.

phrases.english: it is with the denial that he should be disqualified!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אִיתָא, בִּכְפִירָה הוּא דְּאִיפְּסִיל לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenge out of the משנה quoted in step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's rule that denial alone makes a שומר a גזלן
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A גזלן is not trusted to swear. The משנה makes someone 'suspect' only through a false oath, so denial alone must not make him a גזלן.

steps.title: The משנה is about a deposit sitting in a swamp
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is about a deposit lying in a swamp, away from the שומר. There his denial is only a way to stall until he can bring it back, so it is not real כפירה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They answer: What case are we dealing with here? When the deposit is lying in a swamp. That is not a real denial, because he is thinking: 'I'll put him off until I go and bring it to him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב ששת by limiting the משנה to a special case where the denial is not a true denial.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת's rule applies when the שומר denies while the item is with him and he plans to keep it. In the משנה's case the item is far away. He only says 'I never got it' to buy time until he can return it. Since he isn't trying to steal, he does not become a גזלן, and he becomes 'suspect' only through an actual false oath.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here? (narrowing a source to a specific case)
A swamp or marsh, far from the שומר's hands
I will put him off / dodge him for now

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that a denial counts as real כפירה only when the שומר means to keep the item. A stalling denial does not make him a גזלן.
steps.whatToRemember: רב ששת stands. A false denial makes a שומר a גזלן only when it is a real denial meant to keep the item, not when he is just stalling because the item is elsewhere.

phrases.english: They say: With what are we dealing here?
Where it is standing in a swamp,
phrases.notes: "It" is the deposited item (like an animal) sitting out in the swamp, not in the שומר's hands right now.

phrases.english: which is not a denial;
because he thinks: I will put him off
until I go and bring it to him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רמי בר חמא's קשיא from steps 31–32.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the משנה deals with a deposit not in the שומר's hands, where the denial is only stalling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה shows that any denial without an oath does not make him a גזלן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a stalling denial (item in a swamp) leaves him not a גזלן. A real denial still makes him a גזלן, as רב ששת said.

steps.title: Proof: one who denies a loan stays a valid witness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the swamp explanation from רב אידי בר אבין's ruling that one who denies a loan is still כשר לעדות.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can see this is true, because רב אידי בר אבין said: someone who denies a loan is still fit to be a witness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is backing up its last answer with a proof. It shows that a denial meant only to stall for time does not make someone a גזלן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A loan is given to be spent, so the borrower usually does not have the money in hand. When he denies the loan, he is only pushing off the lender until he can pay, so רב אידי בר אבין rules he is still כשר לעדות. The case of the deposit lying in the swamp in step 33 works the same way: the denial is a way to stall, not a real attempt to steal.

keyTerms.meaning: "Know it," meaning "you can see this is true." It introduces a supporting proof.
The אמורא whose ruling is brought as the proof
One who denies that he owes a loan
Fit to serve as a witness, meaning not considered a רשע or גזלן

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean lying about a loan is allowed. It only means the lie is treated as stalling, not as stealing, so it does not disqualify him as a witness.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a clear rule from another case: denial that only buys time is not real כפירה. That supports the answer to רמי בר חמא's challenge against רב ששת.

phrases.aramaic: תִּדַּע, דְּאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין:
phrases.english: Know that this is so, for Rav Idi bar Avin said:
phrases.notes: "This" is the point from the last step: denial just to stall for time isn't real stealing.

phrases.english: One who denies a loan
is fit to bear witness.

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּדַּע, דְּאָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the תירוץ of step 33, that stalling denial is not real כפירה, by pointing to a parallel ruling about loans.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a denial made only to buy time, as with the deposit in the swamp, does not make the שומר a גזלן or unfit.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב אידי בר אבין: הכופר במלוה כשר לעדות. A borrower who denies a loan keeps his status as a valid witness, because he is only putting off payment.
